# What Is Organizational Memory, and How AI Changes It

> Summary: Organizational memory, as Walsh and Ungson defined it in 1991, is stored information from an organization's history that can be brought to bear on present decisions. It lives in people, culture, procedures, structures, workplaces and outside archives, and research led by Linda Argote shows it can decay and resists transfer. Organisational memory is the stored information from a company's history that can be brought to bear on present decisions, held in people, culture, procedures, roles, workplaces and outside archives, as Walsh and Ungson defined it in 1991. Research since shows it decays and resists transfer. AI makes retrieving it cheap, but it does not tell an agent which decision is current or why, so the memory still needs an accountable record.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

Organisational memory is the store at the base of **lowob**'s model of the enterprise brain, a loop of store, wiring, record, reasoning and learning. [The enterprise brain is a record, not a mind](https://lowob.com/research/the-enterprise-brain-is-a-record-not-a-mind/) sets out why memory alone is not enough.

## What is organisational memory?

It is what a company can recall to inform a decision now. Walsh and Ungson's 1991 paper in the *Academy of Management Review* defined it as "stored information from an organization's history that can be brought to bear on present decisions."

Argyris and Schön had written in 1978, as Walsh and Ungson quote, that "organizations do not literally remember." Walsh and Ungson accepted that memory is not literal recall, but argued it is real all the same: distributed across people and artefacts, and stored "as a consequence of implementing decisions."

## Where does organisational memory live?

In six places, five inside the firm. The *International Encyclopedia of Organization Studies* (2008) describes this as the traditional framework, five internal archives plus external archives, and later work attributes these "retention bins" to Walsh and Ungson. Linda Argote's 2013 textbook uses the terms "retention bins" and "repositories". The table maps each to a commercial example and to what AI changes.

| Retention bin | What it holds | Commercial example | What AI changes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Individuals | Experience, judgment, who to ask | The account manager who knows why a client was given special terms | Assistants can spread an expert's practice, but cannot recall what was never written |
| Culture | Shared language, stories, norms | "We never discount in the last week of the quarter" | Models absorb the written version of norms, which may lag the lived one |
| Transformations | Procedures that turn inputs into outputs | The approval steps for a pricing exception | Agents can follow written procedures and expose gaps in them |
| Structures | Roles and reporting lines | Who signs off a discount above a threshold | Agent identities and permissions become part of the structure |
| Ecology | The physical and digital workplace | Which channel deals are actually negotiated in | Work moving into chat and calls creates more transcript, not more reason |
| External archives | Records held outside the firm | Clients' copies of contracts, partners' records, filings | Connectors reach some outside sources; most stay unreachable |

The commercial examples and the AI column are **lowob**'s. A seventh bin has arrived since: [agent memory](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-agent-memory/), what an AI system retains between sessions. It records what an agent saw, not what the organisation decided.

## How quickly do organisations forget?

Faster than cumulative experience suggests, on the best-known evidence. How much faster is disputed.

Argote, Beckman and Epple's study of production sites, in *Management Science* in February 1990, reports that "knowledge acquired through production depreciates rapidly" and that cumulative output, the conventional measure of learning, "significantly overstates the persistence of learning." Peter Thompson's 2007 re-analysis of Liberty shipbuilders' wartime records, in the same journal, found rates of forgetting "much smaller than previously reported, and may well be zero." Both concern manufacturing.

Turnover sets the clock for the first bin: the US Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on 24 September 2026 that median tenure with the current employer was 4.1 years in January 2026, falling to 3.0 years for workers aged 25 to 34. In Panopto's survey of 1,000 respondents, reported by HR Dive on 18 July 2018, 42% of institutional knowledge was estimated to be unique to the individual: a vendor survey of self-estimates, so treat it as direction.

## Why is organisational knowledge hard to transfer?

Because much of it is embedded in the interaction of people, tasks and tools, which does not move cleanly.

Argote and Ingram, in *Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes* in 2000, argued that "the creation and transfer of knowledge are a basis for competitive advantage in firms." Their framework held that "interactions among people, tasks, and tools are least likely to fit the new context," so knowledge moves more easily inside a firm than between firms. Argote and Fahrenkopf's 2016 review extended it to members, tasks, tools and networks.

On the commercial line, the reason behind a pricing exception lives in a seller's head, a call and a chat thread. When the seller leaves, the procedure survives without its purpose.

## How does AI change organisational memory?

It makes retrieval cheap and spreads expert practice, but cannot supply unrecorded reasons, and adds two risks.

**Spreading practice.** In a study of 5,179 customer support agents, first issued by NBER in April 2023 and published in the *Quarterly Journal of Economics* in 2025, Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond found an AI assistant raised issues resolved per hour by 14% on average and by 34% for novice and low-skilled workers, with "suggestive evidence that the AI model disseminates the best practices of more able workers."

**Misusing what is found.** The MemTrace benchmark, posted to arXiv on 15 June 2026, tested 13 memory-system configurations and concluded that "the dominant bottleneck is evidence use, not retrieval." When systems failed, the evidence was retrievable ten times more often than it was missing. Finding three versions of a policy is not knowing which one stands; [Supersede, never overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/) sets out how records mark that.

**Summaries replacing sources.** When a summary is the only surviving copy of a meeting, memory narrows to what one model judged important. [Keep the sources, let the summary regenerate](https://lowob.com/research/keep-the-sources-let-the-summary-regenerate/) covers the evidence and the fix.

## What should a company do about it?

Treat memory as the store and build the record on top.

1. **Record decisions where they are made.** Use a [decision record](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/) with the decision, reason, owner, status, expected outcome, check date and falsifier.
2. **Capture reasons at handovers.** A handover that lists open decisions and their reasons protects the individuals bin.
3. **Keep sources immutable.** Summaries and agent memory are views over them, not replacements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Memory serves decisions.** Walsh and Ungson defined it by its use in present decisions, not by volume stored.
- **It lives in six places.** No single system holds it, and AI adds a seventh: agent memory.
- **It decays and resists transfer.** The evidence differs on how fast, not on whether maintenance is needed.
- **AI needs the record.** Retrieval is cheap; knowing which decision is current is not.

## Common questions

### What is organisational memory?

Organisational memory is the stored information from an organisation's history that can be brought to bear on present decisions, in Walsh and Ungson's 1991 definition. It is distributed across individuals, culture, procedures, structures, the workplace and external archives, so no single system holds it. In AI terms it is the store an enterprise brain reads before acting.

### What are the retention bins of organisational memory?

The framework associated with Walsh and Ungson's 1991 paper identifies six: individuals, culture, transformations (procedures that turn inputs into outputs), structures (roles), ecology (the physical workplace) and external archives held outside the firm. Linda Argote's textbook on organisational learning uses the terms retention bins and repositories. AI agent memory can be treated as an additional, newer bin.

### How does AI affect organisational memory?

AI makes stored knowledge cheaper to find and can spread expert practice: one study of 5,179 support agents found a 14% average productivity gain. But it cannot recover reasons nobody recorded, and a June 2026 benchmark found memory systems failed mostly by misusing evidence they had found. Decision records marking the current version address that.

### What is the difference between organisational memory and knowledge management?

Organisational memory is what a company retains from its past, wherever it sits, including people's heads and culture. Knowledge management is the deliberate practice of capturing, organising and sharing some of that memory, usually in documents and knowledge bases. Most organisational memory is never formally managed, which is why departures lose it.

### Why do companies lose knowledge when employees leave?

Because much of it is held by individuals and embedded in how they combine people, tasks and tools, which Argote's research shows does not transfer cleanly. Procedures often survive without the reasons behind them. Median US job tenure was 4.1 years in January 2026, so for most teams this loss is routine rather than exceptional.
